prompt: What makes an alkene react most rapidly as a Diels–Alder dienophile?

choices.text: An electron-withdrawing substituent group
Having no substituents at all, as in ethylene
choices.why: Ethylene itself reacts sluggishly. Reactive dienophiles carry an electron-withdrawing group.

choices.text: A substituent that makes the double-bond carbons more electron-rich
choices.why: Reactive dienophiles have double-bond carbons that are less electron-rich than ethylene's.

choices.text: Being a conjugated diene itself
choices.why: The diene is the other partner. What speeds up the dienophile is an electron-withdrawing group.

explanation: The Diels–Alder reaction occurs most rapidly if the dienophile ("diene lover") has an electron-withdrawing substituent group. Ethylene itself reacts sluggishly, but propenal, ethyl propenoate, maleic anhydride, benzoquinone and propenenitrile are highly reactive.

prompt: Which of these dienophiles reacts most sluggishly in a Diels–Alder reaction?

choices.text: Ethylene, H2C=CH2
Propenal (acrolein), H2C=CHCHO
choices.why: Propenal's aldehyde group is electron-withdrawing, making it a highly reactive dienophile.

choices.text: Propenenitrile (acrylonitrile), H2C=CHC≡N
choices.why: The nitrile group is electron-withdrawing, so propenenitrile is highly reactive.

choices.text: Ethyl propenoate (ethyl acrylate), H2C=CHCO2CH2CH3
choices.why: The ester group is electron-withdrawing, so ethyl propenoate is highly reactive.

explanation: Ethylene has no electron-withdrawing group and reacts sluggishly. Propenal, ethyl propenoate, maleic anhydride, benzoquinone and propenenitrile all have one next to the double bond and are highly reactive dienophiles.

prompt: Which compound named in the section shows that an alkyne can act as a Diels–Alder dienophile?

choices.text: Methyl propynoate, HC≡CCO2CH3
Propenenitrile, H2C=CHC≡N
choices.why: Its triple bond is the C≡N of the nitrile group. The bond that reacts with the diene is its C=C double bond.

choices.text: Ethyl propenoate, H2C=CHCO2CH2CH3
choices.why: Ethyl propenoate is an alkene (an acrylate ester), not an alkyne.

choices.text: Maleic anhydride
choices.why: Maleic anhydride reacts through a C=C double bond; it has no triple bond.

explanation: Alkynes such as methyl propynoate can act as Diels–Alder dienophiles. As in the alkene dienophiles, the triple bond is adjacent to the positively polarized carbon of an electron-withdrawing group, here an ester.

prompt: How does an electron-withdrawing group affect the double-bond carbons of a dienophile such as propenal?

choices.text: It makes them less electron-rich than the carbons of ethylene
It makes them more electron-rich than the carbons of ethylene
choices.why: Electrostatic potential maps show the reverse: the double-bond carbons of propenal and propenenitrile are less electron-rich.

choices.text: It turns the double bond into a single bond
choices.why: The double bond remains; it is just less electron-rich.

choices.text: It has no electronic effect; it only adds bulk
choices.why: The positively polarized carbon of the substituent draws electron density from the adjacent double bond.

explanation: In every good dienophile, the double or triple bond is adjacent to the positively polarized carbon of an electron-withdrawing substituent. As a result, the double-bond carbons are substantially less electron-rich than the carbons in ethylene (Figure 14.5.1).

prompt: Which of these would you expect to be a good Diels–Alder dienophile?

choices.text: 2-Cyclohexenone: a cyclohexanone with a double bond between carbons 2 and 3
3-Cyclohexenone: a cyclohexanone with a double bond between carbons 3 and 4
choices.why: Its double bond is not adjacent to the positively polarized carbonyl carbon, so the C=O group doesn't activate it.

choices.text: Cyclohexene
choices.why: Cyclohexene has no electron-withdrawing group, so, like ethylene, it reacts sluggishly.

choices.text: Methyl 4-pentenoate, H2C=CHCH2CH2CO2CH3
choices.why: Its ester group is two CH2 groups away from the double bond, not adjacent to it.

explanation: A good dienophile has its double bond adjacent to the positively polarized carbon of an electron-withdrawing group. In 2-cyclohexenone the C=C bond is right next to the C=O carbon (carbon 1); in the other compounds it isn't (Exercise 14.5.2).

prompt: The Diels–Alder reaction is stereospecific. What does that mean?

choices.text: A single product stereoisomer is formed
Both cis and trans products form from either dienophile
choices.why: Stereospecific means one stereoisomer forms, and the dienophile's stereochemistry is kept.

choices.text: The product's stereochemistry is the reverse of the dienophile's
choices.why: The dienophile's stereochemistry is retained: cis gives cis and trans gives trans.

choices.text: Only dienophiles that contain a chirality center can react
choices.why: Stereospecificity describes the product: a single stereoisomer forms.

explanation: A stereospecific reaction is one in which a single product stereoisomer is formed. In the Diels–Alder reaction, the stereochemistry of the dienophile is also retained in the product.

prompt: 1,3-Butadiene undergoes a Diels–Alder reaction with methyl cis-2-butenoate, CH3CH=CHCO2CH3. What product forms?

choices.text: Only the cyclohexene with the CH3 and CO2CH3 groups cis
Only the cyclohexene with the CH3 and CO2CH3 groups trans
choices.why: The trans product comes from methyl trans-2-butenoate. The dienophile's cis stereochemistry is retained.

choices.text: A mixture of the cis- and trans-substituted cyclohexenes
choices.why: The reaction is stereospecific: a single stereoisomer forms.

choices.text: No product, because cis dienophiles can't react
choices.why: Cis dienophiles react fine; this one gives the cis-substituted cyclohexene.

explanation: The Diels–Alder reaction retains the dienophile's stereochemistry. Cycloaddition with methyl cis-2-butenoate gives only the cis-substituted cyclohexene product; methyl trans-2-butenoate gives only the trans product.

prompt: 2,3-Dimethyl-1,3-butadiene reacts with methyl trans-2-butenoate, CH3CH=CHCO2CH3, in a Diels–Alder reaction. Which describes the cyclohexene product?

choices.text: Methyls on both C=C carbons; CH3 and CO2CH3 trans to each other on two neighboring sp3 carbons
Methyls on both C=C carbons; CH3 and CO2CH3 cis to each other on two neighboring sp3 carbons
choices.why: The dienophile was trans, and the Diels–Alder reaction retains its stereochemistry.

choices.text: CH3 and CO2CH3 on the C=C carbons; the other two methyls trans on sp3 carbons
choices.why: The dienophile carbons become sp3. The new C=C forms between carbons 2 and 3 of the diene, which carry the two methyls.

choices.text: Methyls on both C=C carbons; CH3 and CO2CH3 as a mixture of cis and trans isomers
choices.why: The reaction is stereospecific, giving a single product stereoisomer.

explanation: Carbons 2 and 3 of the diene, which carry the methyl groups, become the new double bond. The two dienophile carbons become neighboring sp3 ring carbons, and because the dienophile was trans, its CH3 and CO2CH3 groups stay trans (Exercise 14.5.1).

prompt: 1,3-Butadiene reacts with dimethyl cis-2-butenedioate (CH3O2CCH=CHCO2CH3, with the two ester groups cis). How are the two CO2CH3 groups arranged in the product?

choices.text: Cis to each other on adjacent sp3 ring carbons
Trans to each other on adjacent sp3 ring carbons
choices.why: The cis geometry of the dienophile is retained in the product.

choices.text: On the two carbons of the ring double bond
choices.why: The dienophile carbons become sp3. The new double bond forms between carbons 2 and 3 of the diene.

choices.text: A 50 : 50 mixture of cis and trans arrangements
choices.why: The Diels–Alder reaction is stereospecific; only one stereoisomer forms.

explanation: The dienophile's stereochemistry is retained. Its two CO2CH3 groups are cis on the double bond, so they end up cis on the two adjacent sp3 ring carbons of the cyclohexene product, as in Exercise 14.5.4.

prompt: In a bicyclic compound such as a substituted norbornane, when is a substituent on one bridge called endo?

choices.text: When it is syn (cis) to the larger of the other two bridges
When it is anti (trans) to the larger of the other two bridges
choices.why: That defines exo.

choices.text: When it is syn (cis) to the smaller of the other two bridges
choices.why: Endo is defined relative to the larger of the other two bridges. Syn to the smaller one means anti to the larger, which is exo.

choices.text: When it is on a bridgehead carbon
choices.why: Endo and exo describe substituents on a bridge, relative to the other bridges.

explanation: A substituent on one bridge is endo if it is syn (cis) to the larger of the other two bridges, and exo if it is anti (trans) to the larger of the other two.

prompt: 1,3-Cyclopentadiene and maleic anhydride give a bicyclic product with three bridges: a one-carbon CH2 bridge, a two-carbon CH=CH bridge and a two-carbon bridge carrying the anhydride ring. Which product forms?

choices.text: The endo product, with the anhydride ring cis to the CH=CH bridge
The exo product, with the anhydride ring cis to the CH=CH bridge
choices.why: A substituent cis (syn) to the larger of the other two bridges is endo, not exo.

choices.text: The exo product, with the anhydride ring cis to the CH2 bridge
choices.why: That exo product is not formed. Diels–Alder reactions give the endo product.

choices.text: A 50 : 50 mixture of endo and exo products
choices.why: The reactants orient to give the endo product; the exo product is not formed.

explanation: Diels–Alder reactions give the endo product. The larger of the other two bridges is the two-carbon CH=CH bridge (from carbons 2 and 3 of the diene), so in the endo product the anhydride ring is syn (cis) to that bridge, not to the one-carbon CH2 bridge.

prompt: Why does the Diels–Alder reaction give the endo product rather than the exo product?

choices.text: Orbital overlap is greater when the dienophile's electron-withdrawing group lies under the diene's double bonds
Orbital overlap is greater when the two reactants are as far apart as possible
choices.why: It's the reverse: endo results because the reactants lie directly on top of one another.

choices.text: The electron-withdrawing group points away from the diene, avoiding steric strain
choices.why: In the endo orientation, the electron-withdrawing group is underneath the diene double bonds, not pointing away.

choices.text: The endo product forms through a carbocation intermediate that the exo path lacks
choices.why: The Diels–Alder reaction occurs in one step, with no intermediate.

explanation: Endo products result because the amount of orbital overlap between diene and dienophile is greater when the reactants lie directly on top of one another, so that the electron-withdrawing substituent on the dienophile is underneath the diene double bonds.

prompt: Why must a diene adopt an s-cis conformation to undergo a Diels–Alder reaction?

choices.text: Only then are carbons 1 and 4 close enough to react through a cyclic transition state
Only then are carbons 2 and 3 close enough to bond to the dienophile
choices.why: The dienophile bonds to carbons 1 and 4, the ends of the diene.

choices.text: The s-trans conformation has no p orbitals on carbons 1 and 4
choices.why: The p orbitals are still there. In s-trans the ends of the diene are just too far apart to overlap with the dienophile.

choices.text: Only then are the substituents cis about each of the double bonds
choices.why: s-Cis describes the cis-like arrangement about the single bond between the double bonds, not about the double bonds themselves.

explanation: s-Cis means "cis-like" about the single bond. Only in the s-cis conformation are carbons 1 and 4 of the diene close enough to react through a cyclic transition state; in the s-trans conformation the ends are too far apart to overlap with the dienophile p orbitals.

prompt: (2Z,4Z)-2,4-Hexadiene does not undergo Diels–Alder reactions. Why?

choices.text: Steric strain between its two methyl groups prevents it from adopting the s-cis conformation
Its double bonds aren't conjugated
choices.why: The double bonds at carbons 2 and 4 are conjugated. The problem is reaching the s-cis conformation.

choices.text: Its rings lock the double bonds into an s-trans arrangement
choices.why: That's the reason for the bicyclic diene. 2,4-Hexadiene has no rings; steric strain is what blocks s-cis.

choices.text: It is fixed in the s-cis conformation and only reacts with itself
choices.why: That describes 1,3-cyclopentadiene. (2Z,4Z)-2,4-Hexadiene can't reach s-cis without severe strain.

explanation: In (2Z,4Z)-2,4-hexadiene, the s-cis form would push the two methyl groups into each other, causing severe steric strain. The molecule stays s-trans and so can't undergo Diels–Alder reactions (Figure 14.5.2).

prompt: Which of these dienes could not undergo a Diels–Alder reaction?

choices.text: A bicyclic diene whose rings hold its double bonds rigidly s-trans
1,3-Butadiene, which can rotate about its central single bond
choices.why: 1,3-Butadiene can reach the s-cis conformation by rotation, and it is the diene in many of the section's examples.

choices.text: 1,3-Cyclopentadiene, which is fixed in the s-cis form
choices.why: Dienes fixed s-cis are highly reactive; 1,3-cyclopentadiene even reacts with itself.

choices.text: 2-Methyl-1,3-butadiene (isoprene)
choices.why: Isoprene can rotate into s-cis; it is the diene in Worked Example 14.5.1.

explanation: A diene must adopt an s-cis conformation. In a bicyclic diene whose double bonds are rigidly fixed in an s-trans arrangement by the rings, the ends can never get close enough to react (Figure 14.5.2, Exercise 14.5.3).

prompt: Why does 1,3-cyclopentadiene dimerize at room temperature?

choices.text: Fixed s-cis, it is so reactive that one molecule acts as diene and another as dienophile
It is fixed in the s-trans geometry and reacts by a radical chain
choices.why: Its ring holds it s-cis, and the dimerization is a Diels–Alder reaction, not a radical chain.

choices.text: It carries an electron-withdrawing group that makes it an excellent dienophile
choices.why: 1,3-Cyclopentadiene has no electron-withdrawing group. Its reactivity comes from being locked s-cis.

choices.text: Both molecules act as dienes, bonding through carbons 1 and 4 of each
choices.why: In the self-Diels–Alder reaction, one molecule is the diene and the other is the dienophile.

explanation: Dienes fixed in the correct s-cis geometry are highly reactive. 1,3-Cyclopentadiene is so reactive that at room temperature it dimerizes: one molecule acts as diene and a second acts as dienophile in a self-Diels–Alder reaction.

prompt: 1,3-Cyclopentadiene (C5H6) dimerizes by a Diels–Alder reaction. How many hydrogen atoms does the dimer contain?
explanation: In a cycloaddition the two reactants simply add together; no atoms are lost. Two C5H6 molecules give C10H12, with 12 hydrogens.

prompt: What is the key step in the biosynthesis of lovastatin described in the section?

choices.text: An intramolecular Diels–Alder reaction of a triene
A Diels–Alder reaction between two separate diene molecules
choices.why: In lovastatin biosynthesis, the diene and dienophile are parts of the same molecule.

choices.text: The dimerization of 1,3-cyclopentadiene
choices.why: That's the section's example of a self-Diels–Alder reaction, not the lovastatin step.

choices.text: Electrophilic 1,4-addition of HBr to a diene
choices.why: The key step is a cycloaddition, not an electrophilic addition.

explanation: Biological Diels–Alder reactions are uncommon. In the biosynthesis of the cholesterol-lowering drug lovastatin, the key step is an intramolecular Diels–Alder reaction of a triene, in which the diene and dienophile components are within the same molecule.

prompt: In Worked Example 14.5.1, isoprene (2-methyl-1,3-butadiene) reacts with benzoquinone. How are the hydrogens on the two former dienophile carbons arranged in the product?

choices.text: Cis, because the dienophile double bond is cis to begin with
Trans, because the new ring forces them apart
choices.why: The dienophile's stereochemistry is retained, so hydrogens that start cis stay cis.

choices.text: A mixture of cis and trans
choices.why: The Diels–Alder reaction is stereospecific: a single stereoisomer forms.

choices.text: They are lost, leaving a new double bond between those carbons
choices.why: No atoms are lost. Those carbons become sp3 and keep their hydrogens.

explanation: The dienophile double bond in benzoquinone (part of a ring) is cis to begin with, so its two hydrogens remain cis in the product, where those carbons have become sp3 (Worked Example 14.5.1).

prompt: How does an open-chain diene such as 1,3-butadiene reach the s-cis conformation needed for a Diels–Alder reaction?

choices.text: By rotation about the single bond between carbons 2 and 3
By rotation about one of its double bonds
choices.why: Double bonds don't rotate freely. s-Cis and s-trans interconvert by rotation about the central single bond.

choices.text: By cis–trans isomerization of a double bond
choices.why: s-Cis and s-trans are conformations about the single bond. No double bond changes geometry.

choices.text: It can't; only cyclic dienes can be s-cis
choices.why: Open-chain dienes such as 1,3-butadiene reach s-cis by bond rotation. Only dienes held s-trans by rings or blocked by steric strain can't.

explanation: s-Cis and s-trans are conformations about the single bond that joins the two double bonds. Rotation about the bond between carbons 2 and 3 converts the s-trans form of 1,3-butadiene into the s-cis form needed for reaction.
